title: The ten words, part one (Exodus 20:1–11)
hook: no other gods, no idols, God's name in honor, the sabbath kept

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sinai: thunder, smoke, a trumpet growing louder, and a people trembling at the foot. Your line was the mountain shook.

They hang on courthouse walls and in Sunday school classrooms. They've been carved in stone, stitched on samplers, fought over in lawsuits, and turned into a movie with a parting sea. Can you name all ten? And which one comes first? No other gods is a fair guess. But that isn't quite the first thing the voice on the mountain says. Before a single command, there's a sentence about who is speaking, and what he has already done. Today, the first half of the ten words: the ones about God.
screen: `ON WALLS, IN STONE, IN COURT.` → `CAN YOU NAME ALL TEN?` → `WHAT COMES FIRST?`

segments.voice: Here is how the voice begins, in the King James Bible: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." A rescue comes before any rule. You're already free, the text says, and here is how free people live. Then: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." No carved image to bow down to. Don't take God's name in vain, which means more than swearing: don't use the name emptily, or to prop up a lie. And: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Six days of work and a seventh of rest, for you, your children, your servants, the stranger living with you, even your cattle. The reason given is creation: God rested on the seventh day. In Hebrew, Exodus calls them aseret ha-devarim, the ten words. Decalogue is the Greek version: deka, ten, logos, word. And traditions count the ten differently. In Jewish tradition, the opening sentence, I am the LORD thy God, is the first word. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, put no other gods and no images together, and split coveting into two at the end. Orthodox Christians and Reformed and Anglican churches make the images a separate second commandment. Same text, different numbering, and nobody is leaving anything out. What all of them see is the order. The first words point at God. Everything else follows from what you put first.
screen: `A RESCUE COMES BEFORE ANY RULE.` · `NO OTHER GODS, NO IMAGES, NO EMPTY NAME.` · `REMEMBER THE SABBATH.` · `TEN WORDS, COUNTED THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT HAVE NO OTHER GODS BEFORE ME.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last week: what got your first hour, what you checked before anything else, what you arrange everything else around. Name it honestly, without judging, then ask whether it's what you'd choose to put first. If you pray, you can hear the opening line again, I am the LORD thy God; if you don't, simply hold the question.
Decalogue. Greek for the ten words, the Bible's own name for the commandments given at Sinai. The first ones are about God.
Your line: first things first. The ten start with a rescue, not a rule. That's day three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism classes and Sunday schools, and some churches read them aloud in worship; Catholic and Lutheran catechisms number them one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches another.

chat.says: What's the very first thing said in the ten commandments?
options: Before any rule, who is speaking: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of Egypt.
Thou shalt not kill, since protecting life had to come before everything else.
Honor your parents, because the family had to come before any worship.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed a textual error: Exodus 20:10 names 'thy cattle', not a donkey (the ox and ass are in Deuteronomy 5:14); cut the unsourced statistic 'most run out somewhere around six' and its screen head; cut 'the longest one' and 'here's something many people don't know'; 'the Bible itself never calls them the ten commandments' replaced with what Exodus 34:28 does say; 'most other Protestants' narrowed to Reformed and Anglican churches in voice, myth, trapdoor and howItsDone. Keeper: confirm the three numbering groups.

Numbering: Jewish tradition (20:2 as the first word, 20:3–6 as the second); Catholic and Lutheran (Augustinian: 3–6 as one, coveting split in two); Orthodox and Reformed/most other Protestants (Philonic/Origen: images separate, coveting one). The script says 'most other Protestants'; confirm the grouping and that Anglicans and Reformed fit it.

'Aseret ha-devarim' (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4); note the KJV renders it 'ten commandments'. The script says 'the Bible itself never calls them the ten commandments in Hebrew'; confirm the phrasing.
'Taking the name in vain' glossed as using it emptily or to prop up a lie (Hebrew lashav, 'for emptiness/falsehood'); confirm.
Sabbath reason in Exodus 20:11 is creation; Deuteronomy 5:15 gives the Exodus. The script mentions only Exodus' reason.
